job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Yara Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my parents above their pizzeria in Bologna, so my mornings smell of dough. I wake up, open my laptop, and ask an AI assistant to help me tidy my applications and plan the day. Then I work on a side project, an app that reads menus aloud for blind people, and I send out a few applications. Evenings I help my dad with the till or meet friends from my software engineering course.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did the degree end, and what did you do during the internships?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My final project was the menu reader, and it got the top mark. I did one internship at a fintech start-up, where I wrote tests and fixed small bugs, and one at a big bank, where I learned how slowly big firms move. I've been looking for six months. I'm not worried yet, but I admit I wonder why a top student with two internships hasn't found a seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, this is a nice, steady world where people still matter. I use AI daily already, and honestly it saves me an hour or two, but it doesn't replace thinking. I'd tell friends to use the tools without worshipping them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm relaxed about AI in this world. What I'm less sure of is the job market, because plenty of openings exist but they all want someone with experience. Still, my savings and my parents' support give me time to be choosy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying, finish the menu reader and publish it free on the app stores. I'd contact two charities for blind people and ask for feedback, which could turn into a reference. I'd also freelance small websites for local shops, to earn something and show I can ship real work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I'd feel stable, with a boring but fair job market ahead. Nothing in it frightens me, and I'd even feel a bit lucky that I'm at the start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of your work already runs through AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If everyone uses an assistant, how does a junior stand out?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the extra calm if AI stays small?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good question. I'd say I stand out by shipping something that real people use, not just exercises. A published app with reviews tells a hiring manager more than a clean grade sheet. And I can explain every line of it, with or without help from the assistant.

say: I'd say it's a steady world where people still **matter**, and tools help without replacing thinking.
I'd tell friends to use AI **without worshipping** it.
think: I'm relaxed about AI, but the **job market** still wants experience I don't have.
My savings and my parents' support let me be **choosy**.
do: Finish the menu reader and publish it **free** on the app stores.
Ask two **charities** for blind people for feedback and a reference.
Freelance small **websites** for local shops to show I can ship.
feel: **Calm**, with a fair, boring market ahead, and a bit lucky to be at the start.
S0.quote: A published app with reviews tells a hiring manager more than a clean grade sheet.
fieldNote: She already uses **AI** daily and treats it as a helper, not a threat.
Her answer to the experience trap is to **ship** real work.
Calm is earned by savings, a family business to fall back on and many openings.

steps.text: Publish the menu reader free on the app stores this month
Send three tailored applications a day to Bologna software firms
Build one more small project with an AI coding assistant

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to adapt. Everyone should learn the tools, and companies should retrain their staff instead of cutting them. I'd tell my friends that being able to guide an AI is the new basic skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel a squeeze. Junior coding and testing are the things I'd have done in my first year, and software does a lot of that today. But I'm good at the next layer, like deciding what to build and checking if it's right, and I use AI every day, so I'm ahead of many people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd aim for companies that use AI heavily and need people to direct it, such as product teams and accessibility specialists. I'd show my menu app with a short write-up of how I used AI to build it. I'd also take a short course in product design, three evenings a week, so I'm not just a coder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A mix of excited and uneasy. It's like starting a new language: awkward, but I can learn it. I'd be more worried for friends who don't use the tools yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which tasks of a junior developer does the assistant already do for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tests, boilerplate code, first drafts of documentation. It does those faster than I do. What I do better is talking to a blind user and understanding what they actually need. That's where I'd push my career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you change your plan if junior roles got scarce?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move toward product and accessibility roles, where you need to talk to people and decide what matters. If those are scarce too, I'd go freelance, because I already have a first client, a pizzeria with a messy ordering page.

I'd tell friends that guiding an AI is the new **basic skill**.

I use AI daily and can **decide** what to build, so I'm ahead of many.

Show my menu app with a **write-up** of how I used AI.
Take a short **product design** course three evenings a week.
feel: A mix of **excited** and uneasy, like starting a new language.
S1.quote: What I do better is talking to a blind user and understanding what they actually need.
fieldNote: She treats AI skill as a **baseline** and looks for the layer above it.

steps.text: Write up how I built the menu reader with AI help
Apply to product and accessibility teams at Italian software firms
Take a three-evening-a-week product design course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to act fast. Governments should start income support and retraining now, and companies must share what they know. I'd also be loud online, because silence helps nobody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it frightens me. My field is the first to be done by AI, and two years isn't enough for even one proper job. But I'm not helpless: I understand the tools, and someone has to direct them, at least at the start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd become the person who helps small businesses use AI. I'd offer my services to pizzerias, bakeries and shops in Bologna, charging a fair price. I'd also apply for any job that needs a human who understands the tools, and put my savings into a safe account. If the economy shakes, I'd help in my dad's pizzeria and keep my skills sharp on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but also curious. I can't stop thinking about it, but I don't freeze. It feels like standing on a fast train, hoping the next stop has a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years, and then robots too. What does your plan look like on the day you hear this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say don't worry about my rent, I can help with the till and my own small jobs. Maybe it's a chance to turn the pizzeria into the place where I test ideas for small shops. My dad would say it's crazy, but he likes crazy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents at the pizzeria?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My plan is to become useful before I become unemployable. If AI does everything in two years, the only answer is to be the person who sits with a baker and makes the software fit their kitchen.

say: I'd say we must act fast with **income support** and retraining, and I'd be loud online.
I'd insist companies **share** what they know about the tools.
think: My field is the first AI does, and two years won't give me even one proper **job**.
I understand the tools, so I can be the one who **directs** them.
do: Offer AI help to pizzerias, bakeries and shops in **Bologna** at a fair price.
Apply to any job that needs a human who understands the **tools**.
Put savings in a safe account and help at the family **pizzeria** if needed.
feel: **Anxious** but curious, like standing on a fast train.
S2.quote: My plan is to become useful before I become unemployable.
fieldNote: Her instinct is to become the **local helper** for small shops.
She keeps the family pizzeria as a **safety net**.
Fear is real but she keeps moving.

steps.text: Offer ordering and menu automation to five Bologna pizzerias and bakeries
Apply to firms that need people who direct AI systems
Move savings into a safe account and track monthly spending
Work shifts at my parents' pizzeria while freelancing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to turn it into an opportunity. We should invest in training now, and companies should give graduates real tasks. I'd be positive in public and quietly practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be uneasy but hopeful. I could land a first job, learn from real teams for three years, and be a person who knows the tools before AGI arrives. That's a head start most people won't have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the best first job I can get, then keep my side projects going. I'd save a good chunk each month, maybe a third of my pay. And I'd study part-time, maybe machine learning safety or product design.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less scary than two years. It's like a long exam, where you know the date and can plan. I'd still feel nervous some nights, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years change for someone starting out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I think, but markets alone will leave people behind. I'd want public rules about retraining and a fair share of the gains. Still, I'd prepare as if nobody will save me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think rules or markets will sort this out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big change is that I can build a safety net. With five years, I can save enough for a year of rent and food, and that makes risk-taking possible. I'd also help my parents modernise the pizzeria, so the family has a business that doesn't rely on one salary.

say: I'd say five years is enough to turn this into an **opportunity** if we train now.
I'd be positive in public and quietly **practical**.
think: I'd be **uneasy** but hopeful, with three years of real team experience before AGI.
That's a **head start** most people won't have.
do: Take the best **first job** and keep side projects going.
Save a third of my **pay** each month.
Study part-time **product design** or machine learning safety.
feel: **Less scary** than two years, like an exam with a known date.
S3.quote: With five years, I can save enough for a year of rent and food, and that makes risk-taking possible.
fieldNote: Time becomes **runway**: savings first, then risks.
She wants to help modernise the **family** business too.
Public rules matter to her, but she plans as if nobody will help.

steps.text: Take the best graduate job offer in Bologna and learn on the team
Save a third of every pay cheque for a year of runway
Study part-time product design in the evenings
Modernise the pizzeria's ordering system with my parents

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is great news, a long time to learn and build. I'd tell friends to explore, try several things and not rush. I'd also say we need to protect people who can't adapt as fast as us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm calm. By 33 I could have run my own small company, or been a senior product person. Tools will change many times, and I'm used to that. I'd treat this as a long game with room to grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work in a good first job for three or four years, then start my own business with accessibility tools. I'd buy a small flat, possibly in the neighbourhood by the pizzeria. I'd also save money, but I'd take bold risks, since I have time to recover from a mistake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty hopeful. It feels like being given a long summer to build a boat before the sea comes up. I'd still check the weather every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what would your career look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the pizza. If robots make pizza at home in 2039, my parents' place will have lost something, and so will I. I'd want a human place that stays, even if it isn't efficient.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd be sad to lose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want my parents to retire comfortably before robots change their trade. Ten years gives me time to help them, and that matters more to me than my own title.

say: I'd say ten years is **great news**, a long time to learn and build.
I'd tell friends to **explore** and not rush, and protect people who adapt slower.
think: I'm **calm**: by 33 I could run my own small company.
I treat this as a **long game** with room to grow.

steps.text: Work three years at a product team, then found an accessibility start-up
Take a first job in Bologna and learn the product side
Save a deposit for a flat near the pizzeria

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most, because there is no space to build a career. What would help is public support while we retrain, honest information from companies, and people who give a first chance to graduates.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Adaptable doesn't mean unafraid. I use AI every day and still get scared. Being curious is a way to keep going, not a way to avoid the fear.

portrait: Yara is **23**, a top software engineering graduate in Bologna, living above her parents' pizzeria.
She uses AI **every day**, builds an app for blind people and treats the job hunt as a project.
She feels squeezed in the short scenarios but sees **opportunity** when time is longer.
She leans left, wants public support and retraining, and plans as if nobody will **rescue** her.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI picture, because there would be no time to build a career.
whatWouldHelp: Public support while retraining, honest information from companies and a **first chance** for graduates.
